title: MLS Aims to Convert World Cup Fever into Long-Term Fan Growth
summary:
As the 2026 World Cup concludes, Major League Soccer (MLS) is launching an ambitious effort to capitalize on the tournament's momentum. The league's new campaign, "Thanks World, We'll Take It From Here," features a star-studded commercial starring Lionel Messi that aired during the semifinals and will run during the final.

MLS has been working for decades to grow its fanbase. From 10 teams in 1996, it now has 30 teams — matching the NBA and MLB. Every game is televised on Apple TV. But the World Cup presents a unique opportunity to attract casual sports fans who might not have considered soccer before.

The Chicago Fire, for example, invested nearly $3 million to create a massive watch party at a bar called Recess. Despite Chicago not hosting any World Cup games, over 60,000 people attended the watch parties. "We had a decision to make," said Dave Baldwin, the Fire's president. "One was to bury our head in the sand, or rally behind it."

Twenty-two MLS clubs are running a "First Match on Us" promotion, offering free tickets to first-time attendees. Brian Bilello of the New England Revolution noted that in the 1990s, many sports fans dismissed soccer. "That doesn't really exist as much anymore," he said. The Revolution hosted World Cup matches at Gillette Stadium and a pre-World Cup friendly between France and Brazil.

Since Lionel Messi joined Inter Miami in 2023, MLS attendance and viewership have risen. The league hopes that by converting World Cup excitement into regular season attendance, it can sustain growth for years to come.
why_it_matters: The growth of soccer in America shows how major events can spark lasting new interests. For you, it could mean more opportunities to play, watch, or even one day work in a sport that is becoming part of everyday life.

background_read: Major League Soccer (MLS, the top professional men's soccer league in the United States and Canada) was founded in 1993 and began playing in 1996 with just 10 teams. The 1994 World Cup, which the U.S. hosted, had sparked enough interest to launch the league, but soccer has long struggled for attention in a country dominated by American football, baseball, and basketball. Today MLB has grown to 30 franchises across the two countries, with matches broadcast exclusively on Apple TV thanks to a 10-year streaming deal. The arrival of global icons like David Beckham in 2007 and later Zlatan Ibrahimović raised the league's profile, but nothing compared to the explosion of interest when Lionel Messi signed with Inter Miami in 2023 — doubling ticket sales and viewership. The 2026 World Cup, co-hosted by the U.S., Canada, and Mexico, offers the biggest possible shop window to convert casual watchers into regular league followers. Teams like the Chicago Fire (named after the Great Chicago Fire of 1871) are trying creative ways to ride that wave, even when their city doesn't host any tournament games.

perspectives.description: The 'First Match on Us' campaign and heavy investment by clubs could finally turn curious World Cup watchers into loyal MLS fans. This would mean more revenue for teams, better facilities, and stronger youth academies, building soccer's foundation across North America.

Skeptics argue that MLS has relied too heavily on foreign superstars like Messi to create a buzz, and once the tournament glow fades, many new fans will drift away. Without deep local roots and homegrown stars, the post-World Cup bump may not translate into long-term growth.

History shows U.S. soccer has seen World Cup 'boomlets' before — like after 1994 — that eventually cooled off. However, today's landscape is different: streaming, social media, and a younger, more diverse population might make this moment stick in a way previous waves did not.

The real test will be whether MLS clubs can make the live match experience exciting and affordable enough to keep new fans coming back. Developing top American players who can become household names without needing a Messi-sized star may determine if the league can finally become a permanent part of the U.S. sports scene.
